item.title: The Brand Age, Paul Graham
item.description:
Paul Graham is the co-founder of Y Combinator and one of the great philosophers of the computer science world. For 25 years he has been publishing thoughtful essays on his blog — though infrequently: in 2025, for instance, he published just four pieces. In March 2026 a new one appeared: «The Brand Age». I’d like to discuss it.

Why does this matter to me? Among the writers I follow, Paul Graham comes first. I’ve referenced his essays several times before — in my roundup of resources for product managers, in «The 10 Deadly Sins of a Product Manager», and in «Thinking Through Writing». I’m also drawn to his style: clarifying footnotes and acknowledgments to well-known practitioners who reviewed his drafts. In this latest essay, the reviewers include Sam Altman, among others. And equally important — there’s no advertising, no promotion of any services.

item.title: Product Strategy ≠ Template
item.description:
The goal of strategy is to move from «we build whatever anyone asks for» to a considered position aimed at creating a better future for both users and the business.

As much as we’d like one to exist, there is no universal product strategy template — no template at all, really. The format depends on the company’s maturity, the team’s experience, organizational structure, business model, business strategy, and a huge number of other factors.

item.title: Second Brain: PARA × Obsidian × Granola × Claude
item.description:
A few years ago I organized my notes using the Zettelkasten method in VS Code. A lot has changed since then — largely due to the exponential growth of LLMs and agentic AI. I want to share my current tool stack, which helps reduce cognitive load and keep information from slipping through the cracks when time is scarce: PARA × Obsidian × Granola × Claude.

The article is called «Second Brain,» which means we’re building a system that mirrors the structure of the human brain.

item.title: People Who Write Interestingly
item.description:
I want to share a collection of people on the internet who write interesting content on product-adjacent topics and are worth reading. I often find myself returning to articles by these authors — especially during moments when I’m looking for creative inspiration.

  • Marty Cagan — an iconic figure in the product world and author of a series of widely read books: Inspired, Empowered, and Transformed. Founder of SVPG and a prolific blogger on product management. His ideas about product discovery and empowered teams have become industry standards.
  • Paul Graham — co-founder of Y Combinator and author of remarkable essays that remain relevant across time. He writes about startups, thinking, and decision-making — concisely, precisely, and without filler.
  • Andrew Chen — partner at Andreessen Horowitz and author of a popular blog on growth marketing.
  • Vitalik Buterin — founder of Ethereum and an active blogger. He writes deep technical and philosophical essays on decentralization and the future of technology.
  • Grigory Bakunov — founder of radio-t, former Director of Technology Outreach at Yandex. Writes about technology, management, and life in tech — sharply and without corporate-speak.
  • Oleg Yakubenkov — founder of GoPractice and author of the most popular blog on product analytics in the Russian-speaking world. His simulators and articles are must-reads for anyone who wants to get serious about metrics and unit economics.
  • Artem Gorbunov & Co. — a collection of useful advice on product topics from renowned specialists. Short and to the point — covering writing, interfaces, negotiation, and management.
  • Melissa Perri — author of Escaping the Build Trap. Writes about product as a value system, product culture, and why companies get stuck in feature factory mode.
  • Teresa Torres — author of Continuous Discovery Habits. Her blog covers discovery practices: opportunity solution trees, customer interviews, and the habits of strong product teams.
  • Wes Kao — runs an excellent, practical blog on management, product thinking, and career development. Publishes regularly.
  • Ben Thompson — technology analyst and author of the Stratechery blog. Digs deep into the business strategies of tech companies, platform models, and competitive market dynamics.
  • Valeria Rozova — product leader and curator of an article library on product topics, written by graduates of her courses. The articles are highly practical and detailed — a great resource for developing specific product skills.

item.title: Prioritization Methods: ICE, RICE, DRICE
item.description: Eins, zwei, drei… There are endless ways to prioritize tasks. Every product I’ve ever worked on had its own original approach to ranking projects — each with its own quirks. For a quick tour of the methods used at major companies, check out Misha Karpov’s talk at a Yandex product meetup [1]. As for my personal favorites — there’s the energy-based method, where priorities shift depending on how you’re feeling, and the intuitive method, where you just listen to your gut. The only problem is that teams rarely agree to go along with either approach.

item.title: 10 Deadly Sins of a Junior Product Manager
item.description:
This article was originally published on habr.com.

These «deadly sins» can serve as a self-assessment checklist for both junior and more experienced managers.

So, here are the mistakes — and how to fix them.

1. Believing in Multitasking

Every product manager faces enormous flows of information — countless initiatives and product development ideas that no single person can possibly process within the time available. Stakeholders push their agendas, users complain, the calendar is packed with meetings, and the Product Backlog grows by the day.

item.title: Thinking Through Writing
item.description:
I came across a fascinating interview with Andrei Styskin (Director at Amazon, former CEO of the search division at Yandex), in which he talks about some interesting aspects of Amazon’s internal culture — in particular, its «document-centric» approach to meetings and decision-making.

  1. Every work meeting is a collaborative exercise where participants work through a pre-prepared document on a specific problem. Part of the time (10 to 20 minutes) is spent reading the document individually; the rest is spent discussing and commenting on it. If open questions remain after the meeting, another meeting is scheduled in the same format. The process continues until requirements are unambiguously defined and agreed upon by all stakeholders.
  2. Requirements for any product or feature are developed using the «Working Backwards» method — by writing two documents: a «Press Release» and an «FAQ.» Long before launch, the product manager writes a press release that articulates a vision of the ideal outcome, giving the entire product team a north star to orient around throughout development.
  3. All decisions are made through document reviews, not through verbal conversations in meetings or over a smoke break — as often happens in many workplaces.

Reflecting on my time at Yandex (a great company, though not quite in the same league globally — for context, Yandex’s market cap in 2024 was around $10 billion, while Amazon’s was $2 trillion), I can say that Yandex’s internal culture also encourages employees to express their thinking in writing: detailed wiki documentation is standard practice; task tracker descriptions are written out thoroughly; discussions happen in comments; and internal blogs — both public and anonymous — are common. The more senior the person, the more persuasively and concisely they tend to work with text.

item.title: Books and Resources for Product Managers
item.description:
There’s no shortage of materials online for developing product skills and broadening your horizons. But I want to bring together the most useful, practical, and valuable ones. This list is continuously improving — new materials get added, outdated ones removed. I hope you find something worth your time.

Introduction to Product Culture and the Profession

  • Essay «How to Do Great Work,» Paul Graham. An essay by the iconic Paul Graham on how to do your work well — full of advice and reflection. Recommended reading for anyone starting out in their career, not just product managers.
  • Article «Good Product Manager / Bad Product Manager,» Ben Horowitz. A short piece written in 2012 that remains just as relevant today. It gives a solid general picture of what qualities a good product manager should have.
  • Article «Amazon Leadership Principles,» Amazon. Amazon’s 14 leadership principles — the standard expected of managers at the company and a mandatory part of their interview process. If they don’t resonate with you on the first read, it’s worth coming back to them later.

Managing Yourself and Your Teams

  • «Getting Things Done,» David Allen
  • «Jedi Techniques,» Maxim Dorofeev
  • «Herding Cats: A Primer for Programmers Who Lead Programmers,» J. Hank Rainwater
  • «Managing Humans: Biting and Humorous Tales of a Software Engineering Manager,» Michael Lopp

Research

  • «The Mom Test,» Rob Fitzpatrick. Essential reading on customer discovery interviews. People have strong opinions about the approach in this book — some love it, some push back — but everyone’s read it and no one was left indifferent.
  • «Running Lean: Iterate from Plan A to a Plan That Works,» Ash Maurya
  • Video «How to Talk to Users,» Eric Migicovsky (Y Combinator)
  • Video «ABCDX Segmentation,» Artem Azevich (IIDF Accelerator)
  • Video «Market Sizing,» Alexander Skurikhin (IIDF Accelerator, Yandex)
  • producthunt.com

Analytics

  • «Playing the Numbers: How Analytics Helps Video Games Thrive,» Vasily Sabirov. Probably the only book on product analytics written by a Russian author. It reads less like a textbook and more like a conversation with a product analyst.
  • «Say It with Charts: The Executive’s Guide to Visual Communication,» Gene Zelazny
  • GoPractice Blog. Simply an encyclopedia of product analytics and product management knowledge. Exceptionally well-written articles. Best enjoyed slowly, in the evening, over a cup of tea.
  • Free course «Fundamentals of Statistics and A/B Testing» by Yandex Practicum. An excellent introduction to statistics and A/B testing, put together by Practicum’s team of mathematicians.
  • Free course «Fundamentals of Statistics» by Anatoly Karpov. The most popular statistics course in the Russian-speaking internet, where Anatoly walks through both descriptive and inferential statistics in a clear, structured way. It has become a classic in the Russian-language learning community.

Strategy

  • «Good Strategy Bad Strategy,» Richard Rumelt. A foundational book on strategy that explains what good strategy looks like — and what the many bad versions look like. There’s a short summary on my blog.
  • «The Goal: A Process of Ongoing Improvement,» Eliyahu Goldratt

Delivery Management / Backlog Management

  • «Getting Real: The Smarter, Faster, Easier Way to Build a Successful Web Application,» Jason Fried + David Heinemeier Hansson + Matthew Linderman
  • Article «20 Product Prioritization Techniques: A Map and Guided Tour». A detailed overview of 20 techniques for prioritizing your backlog or hypotheses.
  • Article «RICE: Simple prioritization for product managers,» Intercom. The original article from Intercom, where this prioritization method was born. It also includes an Excel template you can put to use right away.

Interviews and Hiring

  • «The Art of Recruitment: How to Evaluate a Person in an Hour,» Svetlana Ivanova
  • «Who: The A Method for Hiring,» Geoff Smart and Randy Street
  • «Cracking the PM Interview: How to Land a Product Manager Job in Technology,» Gayle Laakmann McDowell
  • «Decode and Conquer,» Lewis C. Lin. One of Lewis Lin’s books — read the others too if you can.
  • Podcast «Sobes» (Interview)
  • Podcast «Dva Stula» (Two Chairs)

Computer Science Basics

  • Free Python courses «Generation Python». A series of free Python courses from scratch by professional developer and instructor Timur Guev. Timur comes from a generation of mathematicians who scored perfect marks on Russia’s national university entrance exams and a generation of developers who went on to work at FAANG companies. You won’t find better beginner courses than this series.
  • Free SQL trainer at sql-ex.ru. One of the best — if not the best — SQL practice platforms, and it’s free. It has an enormous number of exercises; I recommend working through them to build solid SQL query skills. Don’t let the dated interface put you off.
  • «System Design Interview,» Alex Xu

Data Science Basics

  • Article «Machine Learning for People,» vas3k. A thorough introduction for anyone who wants to finally make sense of machine learning — written in plain language, without formulas or theorems, with real-world examples and solutions.
  • «Machine Learning for Humans,» Vishal Maini, Samir Sabri

Inspiring Stories

  • «Elon Musk: Tesla, SpaceX, and the Quest for a Fantastic Future,» Ashlee Vance. The story of Musk’s rise as an entrepreneur — the obstacles he overcame, the risks he took. Including his trip to Russia in 2001 and his attempt to buy an intercontinental ballistic missile.
  • «Pour Your Heart Into It: How Starbucks Built a Company One Cup at a Time,» Dori Jones Yang, Howard Schultz
  • «The Yandex Book,» Dmitry Sokolov-Mitrich. The story of Yandex’s rise from its origins to its IPO. About the personalities of its founders. About how Sergey Brin and Larry Page came to Moscow in 2003 to acquire the company, but Arkady Volozh and Ilya Segalovich refused to sell — and went on to build the most technologically advanced IT company in Russia.

item.title: The Evolution of Goal-Setting Frameworks: From OKR to NCT
item.description:
I came across an interesting approach to goal-setting — NCT (Narratives, Commitments, Tasks) by Ravi Mehta [1]. What makes it compelling is that it positions itself as an alternative to OKR and could be genuinely useful for many product teams. Before diving into NCT, let’s take a quick look at the history of goal-setting frameworks.

In 1954, Peter Drucker introduced the concept of MBO (Management by Objectives) in his book The Practice of Management [2]. The core idea: set goals at the company level and cascade them down to individual contributors at every level. Many services within Yandex, for instance, still use a similar approach today. They even have a dedicated internal tool for cascading goals called «Golzyatnitsa» (roughly, «the goal keeper»).

item.title: CEO of the Product: How a Product Manager Creates Meaning and Communicates Value
item.description:
This article was originally published on Delovoy Mir.

Technology today is advancing at an accelerating pace — there’s even a concept called «technological singularity,» suggesting that in some hypothetical future, explosive technological growth will fundamentally transform our civilization.

But it’s worth remembering that technology doesn’t enter our lives on its own. It arrives through IT products, built to solve specific problems or address the needs of a particular audience.

Product managers play one of the central roles in this process. They identify real audience problems, devise the best solutions, create new user habits, shape new markets, and articulate new ideas that will remain relevant in the future.

item.title: Tools and Services for Product Managers
item.description:
I want to share the services and tools I use on a daily basis to get work done. Maybe you’ll discover something new and make your workflow a little more comfortable.

Product Awareness and UX

  • ProductHunt — the go-to resource for staying on top of the product landscape: new launches, updates, and the evolution of existing products.
  • UserOnboard — a library of detailed UX teardowns for popular services like Gmail, Instagram, Apple Music, Netflix, and more.

Research and A/B Testing

  • Statista — a knowledge base with up-to-date market analytics and research. A corporate account with access to detailed reports is great to have, but the free version still lets you view the basics.
  • Yandex Wordstat — useful for analyzing user search queries in the Russian-language internet segment.
  • ResearchGate — a massive library of academic papers on virtually any topic.
  • Evan’s Awesome A/B Tools — one of the oldest and most popular online tools for planning and analyzing A/B tests: sample size estimation and experiment result evaluation.
  • GoodUI — a pattern library featuring A/B tests and breakdowns of their results.

Diagrams, Flowcharts, and Graphics

  • Miro — the de facto standard for visual collaboration.
  • Mermaid — a tool for generating diagrams from plain text (code). Integrates with many modern wiki systems: Notion, Google Docs, Confluence.
  • Draw.io — a simple, user-friendly tool for creating more complex diagrams than Mermaid supports. Saves files directly to Google Drive and requires no registration or login.
  • Canva — the best tool for creating visual assets; the free version is more than enough for most straightforward tasks.
  • Emojipedia — an emoji reference for adding a touch of personality to requirements and task descriptions.

Personal and Team Productivity

  • Things — a clean, beautifully designed to-do app for Mac and iOS with minimalist aesthetics and excellent typography, perfect for design perfectionists.
  • Ilya Birman’s Typography Layout — a keyboard layout that makes it easy to type proper typographic characters and symbols quickly (✓≈≠₽x↓−""). If you write a lot and care about how your text looks, give Birman’s layout a try — it’s a joy to use.
  • Obsidian — a note-taking app built around Markdown (.md) files.
  • ChatGPT — a replacement for Google Search.
  • Google Sheets, Slides, Colab — the essential baseline toolkit for any product manager.

Rapid MVP Development and Vibe Coding

  • Cursor IDE — a code editor on steroids that lets you build apps and services with minimal programming knowledge, incredibly fast.
  • GitHub / GitHub Pages — deploy static sites to production quickly and for free.
  • Vercel — deploy more complex services to production quickly and for free.

item.title: The Growth Dilemma of Educational Course Economics
item.description:
Looking at the top edTech companies in the Russian-speaking internet market, I noticed an interesting scaling problem baked into the economics of their courses — one they’ve simply learned to live with. I’m not talking about product-led edTech platforms like Lingualeo, but companies that create educational courses for upskilling or career transitions.

Product EdTech Theorem #1

The absence of deadlines in an educational course leads to ↑ Revenue and ↓ Completion Rate (COR). Conversely, having deadlines leads to ↓ Revenue and ↑ Completion Rate.

item.title: Product Management Is Marketing Management
item.description:
And a product manager is a marketing specialist.

This definition is obvious to people who studied marketing in college. But it’s not always clear to those who came to product management from a technical background.

As someone who came up through the technical side, I long believed that «marketing» was limited to finding promotion channels, communicating product value to users, and selling goods — physical or digital, it didn’t matter. But that understanding of marketing is very, very far from the truth.

item.title: Loyalty ≠ Satisfaction
item.description:
Loyalty

Customer Loyalty is devotion to a brand or product. It means that when faced with comparable alternatives, a user will choose our product. This choice is often emotional — a user who loves a product will recommend it to friends and family.

The standard metric for measuring customer loyalty is the NPS (Net Promoter Score), whose growth positively correlates with sales growth and market share gains. This relationship, combined with how easy the metric is to measure, is exactly what made it so popular worldwide. That said, NPS has its fair share of pitfalls — here’s a good article on the topic: «12 подводных камней Net Promoter Score».

item.title: On Leadership
item.description:
The original interview was published on VC.


— Konstantin, why do you think being a leader is worthwhile or interesting?

— Let’s start with what leadership actually is. There are many different definitions — Peter Drucker, for instance, wrote: «Leadership is the ability to help a person move beyond their own limitations.»

Leadership is the skill of positively influencing people in a way that enables a group to achieve ambitious goals through the contribution of each individual member.

item.title: Calculating Classic, Rolling, and Full Retention in Python
item.description: In this post, I want to walk through how to manually calculate 3 types of Retention metrics using Python and Pandas, and how to plot a Retention curve using Matplotlib. Most of the time, a product manager would use an analytics platform for data and metrics analysis — but let’s imagine our PM has been stranded on a deserted island with nothing but a Python interpreter and a handful of libraries. That’s exactly what we’ll use.

item.title: Chart Templates for Data Visualization
item.description:
Product managers present constantly: they finish a research study → share the findings; a new quarter kicks off → announce goals; a quarter, half-year, or year wraps up → review results; and so on.

Data visualization tends to be the weak spot in these presentations, so I put together a Google Sheets template where I’ll collect and update reference chart examples for the most common product, business, and financial data.

item.title: The Zettelkasten Method of Note-Taking
item.description:
Zettelkasten is an increasingly popular method of organizing notes and ideas, developed by the extraordinarily productive German sociologist Niklas Luhmann, who over his lifetime managed to write more than 70 major academic books and 500 scholarly articles, and received prestigious doctoral honors and prizes for his contributions to sociology.

The Zettelkasten note-taking method helped Luhmann acquire new knowledge more effectively and engage in deep research work. This gives rise to the hypothesis: «If Zettelkasten helped Luhmann absorb new knowledge, it can help us too.» All that’s left is to put this promising hypothesis to the test.

On English- and Russian-language resources online, Zettelkasten only started gaining attention in 2020, following the publication of David Clear’s article «Zettelkasten — How One German Scholar Was So Freakishly Productive,» which has a Russian translation on Habr. This is despite the fact that Luhmann never kept his unique knowledge management method a secret — detailed descriptions of it in the original can be found in German journals from 1981 to 1987 (originals in German).

item.title: How to Run a Retrospective for a Large Team
item.description:
A retrospective is a group reflection exercise — a tool for continuous improvement and cultural change within a team.

Most of us hear about «retros» in the context of end-of-sprint ceremonies in iterative development. However, the vast majority of teams don’t follow Scrum or any iterative approach to building software products. That’s no reason to abandon self-reflection or group reflection when you hit key project milestones.

Below is a detailed 8-step plan with timings for running an engaging retrospective with a large team (10+ people).

item.title: ICE, RICE, DRICE Prioritization Template
item.description:
A Google Sheets template for prioritizing product initiatives using three methods: ICE, RICE, and DRICE. For a deeper dive into the methods, see the article «ICE, RICE, DRICE Prioritization Methods».

What’s inside

  • Confidence (confidence in the estimate)

item.title: On the Certified Scrum Product Owner Certification
item.description:
In his book Empowered: Ordinary People, Extraordinary Products, Marty Cagan recommends that aspiring product managers get CSPO training and certification early in their careers. I want to share what you can actually expect from this training — beyond just another badge to collect (and a fairly pricey one at that).

The training runs two full days. The first day covers the fundamentals of Agile and Scrum through group exercises, with a brief overview of other product development methodologies. For those just entering the profession, this day is genuinely valuable — it builds a deeper, more intentional understanding of Scrum. That knowledge is useful as a foundation for evaluating and comparing the processes at your own company or on your product.

More experienced product managers will find it helpful for formalizing and structuring what they already know. Most of us work directly with development teams, and a fresh perspective can spark new ideas around creativity and engagement within the team.

item.title: Personal Consultation
item.description:
For those just starting out — I’ll help you understand how the product manager role works, what managers expect, and what core competencies matter. After the session, you’ll have a clear picture of what’s missing for a confident start and how to build your own development plan. I can help you review or write your resume and prepare for case interviews to land the job you want.

For experienced product managers — I’ll help you assess your current grade level and put together a personal development plan. We’ll work through key competencies, identify growth areas, and map out concrete steps to move to the next level in your career. I can also help with questions around structuring your product process and defining the right product metrics.
